#8593. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment)

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more quickly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45)

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the big tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:

Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

Is Buy and Hold Always the Best Strategy? History Says… Not Always. Yes, over the last few decades, the buy-and-hold strategy has worked incredibly well, with U.S. stock markets delivering strong returns. But that hasn’t always been the case. There have been entire decades where buy and hold yielded little to no real returns—or worse.

The 1930s: The Great Depression saw the Dow Jones lose nearly 90% of its value from 1929 to 1932. Even though the market eventually recovered, it took 25 years (until 1954) for stocks to fully regain their pre-crash levels.

The 1970s: Stagflation (high inflation + stagnant growth) crushed stock returns. The S&P 500 gained only 5% total from 1969 to 1979, which was a negative real return after inflation.

The 2000s: After the Dot-Com bubble burst in 2000 and the Financial Crisis of 2008, the S&P 500 produced negative total returns from 2000 to 2009—dubbed the “Lost Decade” for stocks.

While stocks historically tend to rise over long periods, these examples show that timing, valuation, and diversification matter. Simply buying and holding without considering macroeconomic conditions or valuations can lead to lost decades for investors

Mr. Money Mustache February 25, 2025, 10:34 am

Some of those stories about past periods of low stock returns are true, but I encourage readers to remember three more things:

1) They are usually cherry picked, for example starting from the exact peak of the 1929 bubble. In reality, investors at the time had probably accumulated most of their investments at lower prices, so they were net-positive far sooner than 1954

2) Many of the analyses you see online happen to leave out the most important reason we own stocks in the long run: DIVIDENDS – so ensure that any past simulations you run are using a data set that includes dividends (Nick Maggiulli from Of Dollars and Data is a great author who understands this: https://ofdollarsanddata.com/sp500-calculator/)

3) It’s easy to tell stories about the past and imagine that we all have a crystal ball. But remember that people back then had NO IDEA when the crash would come. In fact, I have been receiving emails non-stop since I 2013, shortly after I started writing this blog stating that it’s “time to go to cash because the market is overvalued”. In retrospect, not only our share prices but our economic growth and company earnings have been spectacular since then.

And perhaps most importantly 4) Ten years is a TINY time horizon to be thinking about investment performance for FIRE people. I’m personally less than a third of the way through my seventy year retirement, so I think in much longer time periods. A 10-15 year stretch of minimal stock growth is all built into the safety margin.

There is definitely a limit to how much a nation can safely borrow as a percentage of GDP. But this is very different from the crap the politicians sling around to rile up their base and justify cutting the programs they just happen to dislike for ideological reasons.

In a worldwide currency and debt market like we have, if you borrow too much the market sends you a signal in the form of lower demand for your dollars which leads to a decline in your currency’s value. Then you need to offer higher interest rates in order to keep borrowing money.

In recent decades the US has had the opposite “problem” – we issue higher and higher amounts of debt for sale, and buyers keep vacuuming it up which keeps our dollar strong. So like a drunk teen at the liquor store with his Mom’s credit card, we keep taking advantage of the free sauce.

To the extent that our government uses this borrowed money to build infrastructure that actually helps our country: transportation networks, ports, power production, educating our populace, even incentivizing things like Arizona semiconductor fabs, we are actually getting ahead because we are using other people’s money to build our own wealth.

It can also help to use this implicit subsidy to just lower taxes on businesses and average workers, because this will trigger more company formation and wealth and employment.

But if we go too far and see our dollar drop more than we want *or* lose our status as the world’s reserve currency, we will have to go on a serious spending diet.

But the issue is best discussed by a group of well trained economists and business leaders with a set of spreadsheets rather than a shouting political candidate at a rally.

The best approach is somewhere in between: run a sensible budget, but also bend the rules a bit and borrow a safe amount for the long run to continue juicing our own economy.

In practical terms, this means a 4% initial withdrawal did eventually work out for a 1970s retiree but only because subsequent decades (the 1980s and 1990s) were very strong. The retiree would have seen their nest egg shrink alarmingly in the first 5–10 years, likely coming close to depletion by the early 1980s, before the tide turned. T. Rowe Price analysts, for instance, note that a 1973 retiree’s portfolio (with a roughly 4% starting withdrawal) began at $500k, sank to ~$328k by 1974, but then recovered to over $500k by 1982 and ultimately grew to over $1 million by the end of 30 years​ TROWEPRICE.COM ​ TROWEPRICE.COM . In hindsight the 4% rule “worked” for that retiree – but if inflation had stayed high longer or if the 1980s boom had been weaker, the outcome could have been a failure.

It’s not a coincidence that the 4% rule just barely worked for 1970s retirees. That was the worst time period for investors in the 20th century, and 4% was chosen because it’s the maximum withdrawal rate that survived even that period.

The thing that I find interesting is all the doomsayers (i.e., those prognosticating some sort of nigh-apocalyptic destruction of the stock market) seem to operate under this bizarre assumption that the behemoths (i.e., the Magnificent 7 and others near the top of the pile) are just going to sit there and allow themselves to get trampled by some upstart. Or that they will just shrug their shoulders, say something like “well, I guess it was fun while it lasted, time to pack up the toys and go home” and then it will all be over.

Will there be disruption? Absolutely! Will it somehow upend the US stock market? I highly doubt that. The companies in the S&P 500 are economic engines, and their fuel is not just natural resources from Canada, Brazil, and Russia, but also other smaller companies. As soon as some small company comes along with a potentially disruptive change, you will absolutely see the big boys try to get in on the game (both by attempting to acquire the upstart, and also by starting or accelerating their own efforts in that space).

There is a good chance that some of the economic benefit will be “lost” (i.e., those who get in early will reap an outsized gain, while those of us index-only investors will have to wait for that disruptive technology to go mainstream), but in the end that disruptive technology will become *part* of the engine of our economy, rather than wrecking it.

My question is what happens in countries where monopolies control those things and stomp out competition due to undue bought influence from the government? In that case, the naturally self-correcting mechanisms don’t work, and political capital controls the top companies, rather than true innovation driving the market.

I suppose those companies would still be making record profits, though, so it may be a moot point.

Y axis is S&P500. On x-axis, Year 0 means “right now”. The x-axis means “future”. The red line starts below yellow and blue because stocks are overvalued, i.e. have a higher P/E. The red shows what S&P SHOULD BE if P/E was typical, not very high as it is now. Basically, if the market crashed right now and reversed to a normal P/E. The blue line shows what S&P would be in the future if the current trends continue (unlikely). As mentioned above, the red line shows what S&P future will be if stocks would suddenly revert to a typical P&E now. The yellow line is similar to the red line, but shows a more gradual reversal to typical P/Es, over time. M&Ms point is that even the worse case scenario – red line – is still pretty good.

Any other economists (certified or armchair) want to weigh in?

Thanks for that Paul! I feel vindicated by your ChatGPT report. I also feel a bit silly for not consulting AI first!

One other thing I was thinking about this morning that may be affecting PEs: private equity. Consider SpaceX and Stripe. If they were public, they’d have 9 figure valuations. And more companies are staying public longer. Or maybe forever. If a company doesn’t need the capital, why deal with the hassle of being public?

So, more companies are staying private longer or maybe forever. But I could see this driving PEs down since a company like SpaceX would have an aggressive valuation. Or maybe it’s driving PS up since the overall market cap of the public markets is smaller.

Dunno! But I enjoy thinking about this stuff.

I particularly agree with the part about the relationship between low interest rates and higher PEs. The US (and global) has had low rates for such a significant period of time which may have moved the PEs higher. With rates now finally reaching levels last seen in 2008, and before 2000s, it will be interesting to me as to whether that starts to finally filter into the PEs once the market forecasts that rates will remain at this level.

I took off from work to go snowboarding with my childhood best friend and I get MMM article on the same day. Doesn’t get much better than that. Great article and thanks for your insights.

Some context regarding the accuracy of Vanguard’s previous predictions: https://www.mymoneyblog.com/vanguard-10-year-stock-market-forecast-2025-2035.html TL:DR – not accurate.

I must admit it does feel a bit like 1999. Even if I had a crystal ball, I’m not sure I would do much differently. In December and again in January I took some tech stock profits off the table. I’m now sitting on what I like to call my five year emergency fund. it’s earning 4% interest and it feels sort of good to have as a bridge over troubled waters if needed. And it’s never a bad idea to follow Warren Buffett’s lead.

It sounds weird, but I’m kind of glad to be getting old. Most of this AI stuff is not really going to affect me too much. I retired early on MMM’s recommendation. Fortunately I’ve been investing in the stock market since the early 90s, so I can’t even remember how many times the money has doubled (Hint:start EARLY kiddos!). I feel blessed to have mostly dodged the major financial bullets over the decades, but either way, the key was to stay fully invested and diversified throughout the ups and downs.Oh, and NEVER believe the hype or listen to financial pundits and gurus (well, maybe other than the Buffet).

I feel like everything that was promised in the dot com era was eventually fulfilled, just some years after the crash. AI is very promising but the timing of the monetization of AI is the key. I shifted out of US funds and into international funds, particularly a high dividend yield fund with a PE ratio of just 12. The idea for that came from that vanguard forecast you mentioned. I read another report, from fidelity I think, that said international would outpace US stocks for at least 20 years. Who knows how their models work, but it’s interesting that they are in some agreement.

MMM – Great thoughts here. I am certainly one of those who is concerned about the extremely expensive stock market, and worry that stocks are priced with expectations of incredible golden age type profits being just around the corner.

I love the rational take here, the reassurance that the long-run still offers good returns for even expensive US stocks, and I also like the fact that there is some very reasonable puts around the benefits of paying off a higher interest rate mortgage.

Given that I have spent so much time around real estate, I’m just more comfortable with it, and the “P/E” ration real estate (cap rates) in my local area, relative to the. S&P 500 right now. And, I’m reluctant to and don’t know what I’m really doing when I invest in international stocks.

Thank you, this confirms many of my thoughts so far. I guess we’ll finally see that overdue decade of MSCI World outperforming SP500 before things turn around again for a decade or so. Meanwhile, on the us side, do you think it would make sense to invest preferentially in SP500-MAG7 ? I also look forward to what AI will bring. If done right it will also largely compensate for demographic issues and ageing populations in the developed world.

I’m retired and trying to decide whether to keep my house, or sell it and put the money in VTSAX or similar. Is there a formula for the net rental income that I receive vs safe withdrawal rate if invested in stocks. I’ve been using the 4% rule as how much I should net from my rental house, compared with stocks. For example if I can net $1M selling my house, I could get $40K a year at 4%. If I net more than $40K annually from rent, keeping the house is a better deal. But being a landlord sucks, especially in NYC, so passive income is more appealing, all things being equal. Any advice/comments?

You’d need to calculate your overall return and whether keeping the house+appreciation+rental growth is higher than share dividends + appreciation. What’s the overall net IRR between the two.

Your house could do better since its a small business and you can lever it, but its incredibly location and timing dependent. I’m not a fan of a large property as part of portfolio because of the liquidity issue and I don’t want to be a landlord, but there’s no reason why it shouldn’t do well or better than VTSAX as part of your portfolio.

Dear MMM and all other readers Thank you for getting to the point of the complicated. As you said, it’s just simple math.

Regarding the 330+ billion cash Warren Buffett has invested in short-dated government bonds. Compared to the S&P500 with a P/E ratio of 27.8, the government bonds are yielding 4 to 5% without risk. The S&P500 yields around 3.6% (risky / inverse of 27.8). Here too, it’s just simple math.

There’s was a fascinating article in the New Yorker last year by Ted Chiang: “Will A.I. Become the New McKinsey?”

I would be interested in hearing your thoughts on it.

Any recommendations for a “real return” percentage for a retirement calculator looking ahead 20-30 years. I often hear people using 6-7% real, but based on the current valuations, I’m thinking that may be way too optimistic.

I agree that is too optimistic. 4% is often used based on things like the Trinity Study. I prefer to use William Berstein’s analysis; the expected real return is the annualized growth of the economy in constant dollars, 2%, plus the dividend, currently 1.3% for the S&P 500, for a total expected real return of 3.3% at the current valuation.

I’ve started investing about 8 years ago. I’ve decided, and stuck with, a two prong approach. Half in well known index etf’s, half in about 20 handpicked stocks that I liked. If i screw up myself, I would still have the etf’s. For my own hand picked stocks, I choose to stick to about 20 stocks. Research has shown multiple times that 20 stocks will yield the same results as an index consisting of hundreds or even thousands of stocks. You don’t need an index, you just need 20 random stocks and they’ll perform the same.

My 20 stocks I keep as a hobby and to learn about new companies, how companies are run, new insights etc. It keeps me interested in the stockmarket. The stocks that I pick are companies I’m familiar with, or believe will do well. I avoid hype like the plague. I avoid high PE’s. I try to follow Buffets advice as best I can. Don’t loose money. Buy low, sell never or at least very high.

I’ve sold Tesla at a loss in 2019, never owned it again. I’ve never owned Meta, Amazon, Apple, Nvidia. Or AMD, or any other recent 10bagger. I have stuck with boring, mostly relatively unknown stocks. Or where I saw a real opportunity.

The real kicker? About 70% of the stocks are European. I barely own any US stocks.

The results: My own hand picked 20 stocks have done better than the S&P500.

I’m not a great stock picker. I didn’t invest in NVidia, Google, AMD. I sold Tesla at a loss before it went time 20. I still hold a 50% on a significant Intel stake. I stuck to Europe while the US outperformed. And yet, my returns have beaten the S&P500.

There are some great stocks in Europe. There is also a lot of not so great stocks. Picking the great ones isn’t hard. Most can see the bad ones from far away and avoid them like the plague.

The real problem for Europe, is the lack of representative indexes. The European indexes just simply suck. Not enough stocks in them. Every country has their own indexes of just a few stocks. And maybe an even bigger underappreciated problem comparing the US to the EU: dividends. The US companies barely pay dividends, while EU companies still pay a good deal. The difference adds up over the years, but most indexes don’t compare the total return.

As for these high markets: please keep in mind: we’ve had some serious inflation. Inflation adjusted returns over the last years aren’t out of the ordinary. Especially comparing inflation adjusted returns to something like a zero risk tips ladder.

Your S&P500 without the magnificent seven looks less impressive. But instead of taking out the best performers, maybe do the same but also take out the absolute worst performers. And then do both. You might be surprised to learn the whole market is actually doing really pretty well.

Conclusion: I’m really not worried. Taking a broader look and accounting for inflation and zero risk treasuries, returns aren’t extraordinary. We live in a world where in one generation, huge countries go from poor to rich, and they all want stable investments for their retirements. We live in an age where a growing number of retires will keep demand high because they don’t have to fear for their incomes. House payments look high, but the total mortgage debt in many western countries is actually quite low.

If there ever was a golden age, it’s now. We’re deadsmack in the middle of the best economic boom in history, and it doesn’t seem to be ending anytime soon (if you take a worldwide broad look). Don’t focus too much on the numbers. Look around the world, see how much things are improving in just one generation world wide. You can only conclude demand for stocks will keep increasing, and companies will keep improving profits as demand keeps increasing. Will there be shock and crashes? Sure, but nothing to worry about for a early retiree.

I also like to think of the property pay down as an after tax return, since you need to earn the money first , then pay taxes to pay the mortgage.

On the US vs International shares, people recommending to stay US only, I wonder if there’s bias because the US has done well and whether that position would’ve been very different if we were looking at a period where US had seen a weak decade, like post 08?

Having started investing in real estate before the 18% mtg rates, then watch my collegues sweat out Black Monday Oct 19/87, Iam glad we stayed 100% RE. Passive income allowed me to retire in 1998 & over the years we have also unloaded many high cap. appreciated investment properties, often holding the notes @ 10-12% with a 5yr balloon. We still buy using cash from our 401(k)-solos. Real Esatate has been our ‘annuity’ & has outperformed most of those we know who have invested heavily in the equities market. Over the years the odd bad tenant, bloodied knuckles & rehab costs have never been as stressful as our friends who said they refused to look at their 401(k)’s as the mkt swooned. All have since worked until their late 60’s. In fact my business consultant, equities investor friend, who told us we would go broke in real estate, suffers very poor health & still has to work at 70. Thanks to my wife all of our kids are heavily invested in real estate & have enough passive income to cover their respective mortgages.

Mr. Money Mustache March 3, 2025, 4:38 pm

Hey Pat, thanks for the interesting and very opposite perspective!

I’m glad you’ve done so well with real estate. But I also find it hard to imagine, given the spectacular returns of our stock index for the past century, *anybody* who doesn’t get to retire very early and sleep very well even on a 100% stock portfolio.

Unless they went at it Cowboy Style with an actively managed stock trading approach and gambled all their wealth away?

I think the real answer is what you enjoy doing in your retirement. I learned from managing rental properties of my own in the past, that it kinda ruins my day when there’s a problem with one of my tenant-occupied properties and I have to manage it.

On the other hand, I wouldn’t feel the slightest worry if the stock market dropped 50% in a bad panic or recession. That’s a self-correcting problem that requires no effort from me and just makes most savers wealthier in the long run as our dividends reinvest and our surplus cash flows into the index at discounted prices.

One last thing I like to check in on for any wealthier investors reading this: make sure you continue to question your old habits as your wealth grows.

For example, when you had $250k of real estate, it was appropriate to hustle and add more. When you have $10M of it, you don’t have to do a thing – you could sell it ALL and put it into inflation adjusted bonds for the rest of your life and you’d still be swimming in cash. So only keep doing it if you love the work – NOT for the money.

#8592. 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Editorial Disclosure: Opinions, reviews, analyses & recommendations are the author’s alone, and have not been reviewed, endorsed, or approved by any of these entities.

The scariest thing on a physician’s desk this October is the fourth-quarter estimated tax worksheet, propped against a 403(b) statement that hasn’t moved since spring.

Most retirement articles are written for someone worried about running out of money. You should worry about that too. On top of it, you carry a problem the average saver never meets: a tax code that takes 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700, trims your itemized deductions once you get there, shrinks your SALT break somewhere past $505,000, and reaches two years backward to set your Medicare premiums.

Every mistake on this list costs a little more in that bracket.

This list is built for physicians with six figures before the comma, including those who collect some or all of it on a 1099.

Physicians are one of the few groups positioned to collect the maximum Social Security benefit, because most of you clear the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December. That makes claiming age a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month; the same worker gets $4,152 at full retirement age and roughly $5,181 by holding out until 70. Claiming early trims the benefit permanently (5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months, 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that), and every year you wait past full retirement age adds 8%.

Dr. Addams claimed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums shifts at $200 an hour. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480, so his own paycheck ate his benefit. (Social Security credits some of that back at full retirement age, but the cash-flow plan he built was toast.) Semi-retired physicians are exactly the people who keep earning after they file.

Two other quirks hit doctors harder. The formula averages your 35 highest-earning years, and residency plus a late start can leave early retirees with zeros in that average; the bend points in the formula soften the blow for high earners, but pull your record at ssa.gov before assuming anything.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a price no insurer will match.

A serious diagnosis or a family tree with short branches can justify claiming early. For a healthy 62-year-old internist with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

The textbook move as retirement approaches is to dial down risk. Physicians who take that advice too far end up with a portfolio that can’t outrun their withdrawals.

Run the timeline. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years or longer. A bond-heavy portfolio feels safe in year one and starts losing ground to inflation and withdrawals by year ten, which is why stocks still have to do some of the lifting deep into retirement.

High earners face a sneakier version of this mistake, and it lives in asset location. Taxable bond interest gets hit at ordinary rates. At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (which applies above $250,000 of modified AGI for married couples and has never been indexed for inflation), you hand close to 41 cents of every interest dollar to Washington before your state takes its cut.

Park bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b), hold broad stock index funds in taxable, and look at municipal bonds if you need fixed income outside retirement accounts.

How much stock is enough? That depends on your spending, your other income, and how well you sleep through a 25% drawdown. “As little as possible” is not an allocation.

Landmark Wealth Management puts the S&P 500’s annualized return from 1926 through 2024 at about 10.3%. It’s a lovely number, and nobody in history has received it in a straight line.

Sequence-of-returns risk turns a reasonable plan into a slasher film.

Two physicians retire with the same $4 million and the same 10-year average return. Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (who, it turns out, was not) retires into a bear market, sells shares near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back when prices recover. Same average, very different endings.

The 4% rule tries to account for that. William Bengen published it in 1994: withdraw 4% in year one, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation every year after. Bengen has since revised his own number upward to about 4.7%.

The real mistake is treating any single figure as permanent. Retirees who trim spending after bad years (guardrail strategies) or who keep two to three years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds (the bucket approach) give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Pick a method, stress-test it against a crash in year one, and expect to adjust it.

Read: Is the 4% Rule Too Frugal for Doctors?

Maxing your 401(k), 403(b), and 457(b) during peak earning years at 37% is a good move. The trouble starts when it’s the only move for 25 years.

Dr. Smart retires at 60 with $5 million, nearly all of it pre-tax. Required minimum distributions begin at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security, up to 85% of which is taxable.

Suddenly, a retired doctor is back in a high bracket, paying tax on money she deferred at a high bracket. Then Medicare notices.

Medicare’s IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at a modified AGI of $218,000 for couples ($109,000 single).

At the top tier, Part B jumps from the standard $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, which adds up to roughly $6,900 a year per person in surcharges alone. Medicare also uses a two-year look-back, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

The fix lives in the gap years. Retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade where taxable income is the lowest it’s been since residency. Converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth in that window, filling the lower brackets on purpose, shrinks future RMDs before they become a problem.

During your working years, fund backdoor Roth IRAs ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan.

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already made that choice for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions have to go in as Roth.

Rental income, a part-time medical director role, or expert witness work can also give you an income stream that doesn’t depend on draining one enormous tax-deferred account.

Physicians tend to underestimate retirement spending for a simple reason: they’ve never tracked it. The paycheck covered everything, so nobody looked.

Pull 12 months of actual spending from your cards and accounts, then adjust for what changes after medicine. Disability insurance, licensing fees, CME, and the commute fall away. Travel tends to swell and front-load into the first decade.

Healthcare before Medicare can run five figures a year for a couple buying their own coverage. Long-term care waits at the back of the line: Genworth figures cited in Fisher Investments’ healthcare guide put a semi-private nursing home room at roughly $111,000 a year in 2024, and federal estimates say almost 70% of people will need some form of long-term care, for about three years on average.

Errors cut in two directions. Underestimate spending, and you drain the portfolio early. Overestimate it, and you work three extra years you didn’t need, a loss that never shows up on any statement.

Anyone who practiced through 2022 watched CPI peak at 9.1% that June. Inflation cooled afterward, but prices never went back down.

The damage compounds quietly. A $200,000 annual retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation. Any income stream that doesn’t adjust (a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, a practice buyout paid in level installments) loses purchasing power every year you hold it.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician payment has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 once you adjust for inflation in practice costs. Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched happen to your fee schedule, and build in an inflation assumption a bit above whatever the current forecast says.

The urge to leave is real, and it’s showing up earlier. In Doximity’s physician polling, the share of doctors aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement rose between 2023 and 2026, from 30% to 46%. Among emergency physicians, the figure climbed from 30% to 52%.

Burnout is a legitimate reason to change your life and a poor reason to skip the math. Retiring at 52 instead of 60 means eight fewer years of contributions, eight extra years of withdrawals, and a longer stretch buying your own health insurance before Medicare.

Several costs belong to medicine alone. If your malpractice policy is claims-made, leaving can trigger a tail coverage bill, often priced at a multiple of your annual premium, unless your employer covers it or your carrier offers a free tail at retirement age.

A few years away can complicate credentialing if you want back in, and some boards will ask for a formal re-entry program.

On the brighter side, physicians have unusual access to early withdrawals: governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age, and the rule of 55 lets you tap the 401(k) or 403(b) of the employer you leave in or after the year you turn 55.

A middle path often beats a hard stop. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or moving into a nonclinical role keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow a few more years untouched.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger number, and a market dip convinces you to stay another year, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve thought about slowing down.

Dr. Addams (yes, him again) planned to retire at 62, then 64, then “once the kids finish school.” His youngest graduated in 2019. Money saved after you’ve crossed the finish line buys very little extra safety, and the years spent earning it come out of your healthiest stretch of life.

Hospitals are changing the math as well. Some now require cognitive and physical screening for late-career physicians past a set age, so the decision to keep practicing may not stay entirely yours.

Pick a number and a date, and write down what you’ll do the Monday after. In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those who are simply running from the pager.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

This is the first of three entries that replace the generic advice, and it’s the one high earners ask me about most.

Long-term rentals generate depreciation, but for a full-time physician those losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income.

Short-term rentals play by different rules. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the property isn’t treated as a rental activity under the regulations. Materially participate (most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more hours than any other individual) and the losses become non-passive, free to offset your W-2 or 1099 income.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, permanently restored by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for property acquired after January 19, 2025, and the first-year numbers get large.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, depending on the property and the study. In the 37% bracket, that’s roughly $55,000 to $74,000 of federal tax that stays in your pocket.

The fine print, which the Instagram gurus skip, matters as much as the pitch:

If any of your income arrives on a 1099 (locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work, consulting), you have access to retirement accounts your W-2 colleagues can only envy.

Plenty of contractors open a SEP-IRA and stop there, which is an expensive default.

A Solo 401(k) usually beats it. For 2026, you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (a limit shared with any W-2 401(k) or 403(b) you also contribute to), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings as a sole proprietor, or 25% of W-2 salary through an S corporation, up to a combined $72,000.

Add $8,000 in catch-up contributions at 50, or $11,250 between ages 60 and 63. The employer side stands apart from your hospital plan, so an employed doc with meaningful side income can layer it on top of what they already contribute at work. The SEP has one more flaw for high earners: its balance counts under the pro-rata rule and sabotages the backdoor Roth.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan. It’s a defined benefit plan layered on top of the Solo 401(k), and allowable contributions rise with age, often into six figures a year for physicians in their 50s.

You’ll need an actuary and a funding commitment you can’t skip in a lean year, so it suits consistent earners.

Those deductions do double duty because of the QBI cliff. Physicians run a “specified service trade or business,” so the 20% qualified business income deduction phases out as taxable income rises.

For 2026, married couples get the full deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it vanishes entirely at $553,500 (the single thresholds are $201,750 and $276,750).

Dr. Lucky, married with roughly $500,000 of taxable 1099 income, sits deep in the phase-out. Fund the Solo 401(k) and a cash balance plan, drop taxable income below $403,500, and the QBI deduction rises from the dead on top of the retirement deduction itself.

Self-employment tax deserves a sentence of its own. Contractors pay the employee and employer shares of Social Security (12.4% combined) up to the $184,500 wage base and 2.9% Medicare on everything, plus another 0.9% above $250,000 for married couples.

An S corporation paying you a reasonable salary can trim part of that, though it adds payroll, a separate return, and a salary figure the IRS will scrutinize.

Physicians start saving late. Residency ends somewhere around 30 or 32, often with six-figure student debt, so the compounding years most savers get in their 20s went to call rooms and loan servicers. A year-end cram session can’t make that up.

The calendar matters more than usual this fall. These items won’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

Pick one item from this list before you hand out the first fun-size Snickers, and make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

The Social Security claiming example was eye-opening, since the gap between filing at 62 and waiting until 70 is far larger than most people assume. I also appreciated the warning about stuffing everything into pre-tax accounts, because required minimum distributions and Medicare surcharges can quietly push a retiree back into a high bracket. The practical takeaway for me is to use the gap years for partial Roth conversions instead of leaving the whole tax problem for later.

Turning 70 soon and still earning ~500K. Tell us how starting to receive social security how that will add to income levels, please. I’ll be getting the max.

Thanks for sharing these helpful retirement planning tips! It’s easy to focus on saving money and forget about things like rising costs, unexpected expenses, and how long our savings need to last. Planning ahead and avoiding these common mistakes can make a big difference in the future. I also think it’s important to have the right protection for your work and finances, such as finding a reliable contractor insurance broker when needed. Great article with useful advice that more people should know about!

Great insights here! It’s fascinating how these retirement planning mistakes can ripple into broader financial security issues.

#8589. The Sunday Best (10/18/2026)

As a hospice physician, Jordan Gurmet discusses a familiar tragedy beyond the emotional weight of medical illness: the sudden, overwhelming chaos that unfolds when aging intersects with a lack of intergenerational financial planning.

Aren’t inheritances supposed to be a big deal? All dollars should be treated equally regardless of their source or use, but human brains aren’t wholly rational, and inherited money feels like it should be different from rents, dividends, gains, or earned income. It should be special.

Should we consider claiming Social Security earlier to squeeze more life out of it? Or, put another way, is there a subjective reason why $2000 per month at age 62 is more valuable than $3500 per month at age 70? And is that subjective reason so powerful that it’s worth locking in those lower payments for life?

Stop deluding yourself with the notion that only money will protect and guarantee a great retirement. Building muscle is the cheapest insurance you will ever purchase. It lowers your risk of falls and injuries. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass, is a leading cause of frailty in older people.

#8588. Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

Taxes may be the last thing on your mind right now. The kids are studying for mid-terms and the holidays are almost upon us. But with less than 3 months left in 2026, you have a small window to implement strategies to minimize your tax bill for 2027.

According to Medscape’s 2026 compensation report, physicians earn, on average, $386,000 a year. Primary care physicians earn $298,000 and specialists make, on average, $417,000.

In 2026, a single filer’s taxable income of $256,225 puts them in the 35% bracket. Same for an income of $512,450 MFJ (married filing jointly). The 37% bracket starts above $640,600 for singles and $768,700 for couples.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made permanent many provisions that had been scheduled to expire after 2025. It also added limits and phaseouts that affect higher earners specifically. In this guide, I’ll cover the changes that matter to physicians and what you can do before the year is up.

You can’t always choose when you receive income but some form of income like bonuses, self-employment income, Treasury bill income, and voluntary retirement distributions can be timed to reduce your tax bill for 2026.

Deferring income means you receive it in 2027 instead of 2026, and thus pay the tax a year later. Accelerating work in the opposite way. You can also defer or accelerate deductions to either lower this year’s bill or leave it on the table for next year.

If your employer pays a $20,000 bonus on Dec. 20, it counts as 2026 income. If your employer pays it on Jan. 5, it counts as 2027 income. At a 35% rate, that single date change delays $7,000 of federal tax by a full year.

If you expect to be in the same bracket with lower rates next year, you can defer the bonus. If you think you’ll be in a higher bracket next year, go ahead and take it in 2026.

According to this comprehensive guide by Plante Moran, pushing income into 2027 and pulling deductible expenses into 2026 delays tax, which usually helps. A higher bracket next year means you should take the opposite approach because you pay tax on 2026 income at your lower current rate.

If you’re starting as an attending in 2027, you fit the second group. Taking taxable gains or converting pre-tax IRA money to Roth this year will cost you less than doing it after your pay jumps.

Learn more: The Best Time for Roth Conversions May Be Now

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Employed physicians don’t have much control but ask your group whether it can pay a year-end bonus in January. Locums and 1099 physicians can, however, control invoicing and equipment purchases.

Check your Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exposure before you defer anything. AMT works like a second tax calculation.

First, you calculate your regular tax, then, you recalculate with certain deductions added back, including your SALT deduction. Then you subtract an AMT exemption, which in 2026, is $90,100 for single filers and $140,200 for joint filers. You then must pay whichever tax is higher.

The OBBBA shrank that exemption for high earners in 2026. It starts the reduction at $500,000 of AMTI for singles and $1,000,000 for couples. It then cuts the exemption by 50 cents for every dollar above those thresholds.

The exemption disappears at $680,200 for singles and $1,280,400 for couples.

All that is to say that each extra $1,000 of income inside the phaseout range costs you $500 of exemption, so $1,500 becomes taxable at 28%. That equals a 42% marginal rate, which beats the 37% top regular rate.

Once the exemption disappears, your marginal AMT rate drops to 28%. Estimate your marginal rate for 2026 and 2027, then move income toward the lower-rate year.

Your employer withholds the additional 0.9% Medicare tax only on wages above $200,000, regardless of your filing status or your spouse’s pay. The tax itself applies above $250,000 for joint filers.

Two married physicians who each earn $300,000 have an employer who starts withholding the extra 0.9% Medicare tax once that physician’s pay passes $200,000. Each physician has $100,000 above that line, so each employer withholds $900. Together, the couple has $1,800 withheld.

With a combined wages of $600,000 the joint cutoff is $250,000, so the couple owes 0.9% of the rest of the $350,000. That’s $3,150. After subtracting the $1,800 withheld by the employers, the  couple owes $1,350 more when they file.

You can raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover it. This will require you to submit a new W-4 to your employer and enter the extra amount per paycheck in Step 4(c).

Withholding counts as paid evenly across the year so it beats a late estimated payment. Penalty protection requires payments of at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. The 100% safe harbor covers only taxpayers with 2025 AGI of $150,000 or less, which rules out most attendings.

The annualized income installment method helps when income skews toward year-end, as locums and bonus income often do.

The 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) starts at $200,000 of MAGI for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

Those thresholds have stayed the same since 2013, so every raise adds more of your investment income into the tax. Anything that lowers MAGI, including retirement contributions and HSA deposits, lowers your NIIT too.

The IRS raised the 2026 employee limit for 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457 plans to $24,500. Catch-up contributions add $8,000 at age 50 or older, for a total of $32,500.

There’s also a bonus catch-up of $11,250 for ages 60 to 63, which brings the total to $35,750. If your hospital also offers a governmental 457(b), that plan carries its own limit of $24,500.

SECURE 2.0 now requires employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages to direct catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. That’s all attendings. If your plan offers no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions at all.

Direct Roth IRA contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers.

Employed physicians can contribute $7,500 to a nondeductible traditional IRA and convert it. This works best when neither spouse has funds in a traditional IRA, and you owe tax only on growth between the contribution and the conversion.

A pre-tax IRA balance makes part of the conversion taxable, so roll it into your 401(k) before Dec. 31 if your plan accepts rollovers.

Practice owners have bigger options. A profit-sharing plan allows total contributions of $72,000, or $80,000 with catch-up, or $83,250 at ages 60 to 63.

A SEP allows $72,000 and requires at least $360,000 of self-employment income before the deduction.

A defined benefit plan can allow larger deductible contributions than either, depending on your age and target benefit. The 2026 maximum is $290,000 or 100% of your highest 3-year average earned income, whichever is lower.

Self-employed physicians can set up a plan and make 2026 contributions as late as the tax return due date, including extensions. If you have employees, you likely must let them participate.

Also read: Backdoor Roth IRA 2026: A Step by Step Guide with Vanguard

For 2026, the HSA limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, plus $1,000 at age 55 or older. Contributions reduce AGI and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. A family contribution of $8,750 can save you about $3,063 in federal tax at a 35% rate.

A health FSA is limited to $3,400 and you can carry over up to $680 of unused funds to 2027. The dependent care FSA limit rose to $7,500 from $5,000, which saves you $2,625 at a 35% rate. Those contributions reduce the expenses you can claim for the child and dependent care credit.

Today’s relatively low rates raise the odds that your retirement rate will be higher.

Permanent rates have no expiration date but Congress can still raise them. Converting in chunks over several years keeps each year’s income from jumping into a higher bracket. But a Roth conversion adds to your taxable income in the year you convert so confirm you can pay the tax from outside the IRA.

Early-retired and part-time physicians must now deal with expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit. This means that the ACA cliff now applies to them.

If you earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line, you lose all marketplace subsidies. The threshold is $62,600 for a single person and $129,000 for a family of 4 in 2026.

Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo recommends pairing a high-deductible plan with HSA contributions, which lower your AGI.

Two new rules have reduced the value of itemized gifts.

A 0.5% of AGI floor is now in effect which means a physician with $500,000 of AGI can’t deduct the first $2,500 of donations.

The OBBBA also caps the tax benefit at 35 cents per dollar for filers in the 37% bracket.

Bunching charitable giving can fix most of the floor issue. The floor applies once per year, so 5 years of $10,000 gifts at $500,000 of AGI forfeit $2,500 each year and leave $37,500 deductible.

One $50,000 gift forfeits $2,500 once and leaves $47,500 deductible. The extra $10,000 saves $3,500 at a 35% rate.

Charissa Anderson, a CFP at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management, says that bunching works best when you pair a donor-advised fund with appreciated stock. A donor-advised fund lets you make 1 large gift now and send grants to charities over time.

Plante Moran warns that you should get written acknowledgment that the sponsoring organization holds exclusive legal control of the assets.

If you itemize, shares held for more than 1 year before donating let you deduct full market value and skip the capital gains tax you’d pay otherwise. Most physicians pay 15% on long-term gains plus the 3.8% NIIT, which totals 18.8%.

Physicians with taxable income above $545,500 (single) or $613,700 (joint) pay 20% plus the NIIT, which totals 23.8%. If you donate $50,000 of shares with a $20,000 basis, you can avoid up to $5,640 at 18.8% or $7,140 at 23.8% of the $30,000 gain.

The deduction is capped at 30% of AGI for public charities and you can carry the excess forward 5 years.

Donors can use tax lot selection, as in choosing which specific shares to give. Lots with the largest gains usually make the best candidates. Never donate shares that trade below your basis. Sell them, claim the loss and donate the cash.

Physicians who take the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint) can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts or $2,000 for couples. A couple in the 35% bracket can save $700.

Physicians aged 70 1⁄2 or older can send up to $111,000 from an IRA directly to charity in 2026. That transfer counts toward required minimum distributions and steers clear of taxable income.

For 2026, the SALT cap is $40,400. As your MAGI exceeds $505,000, the cap drops by 30 cents for every extra dollar.

A couple with $550,000 of MAGI have an excess of $45,000. The cap drops by 30% of $45,000, which is $13,500. Their cap falls from $40,400 to $26,900. As your MAGI approaches $606,333, the cap reaches its $10,000 minimum. Above that, it stays at $10,000.

If your 2026 state and local taxes will fall short of the cap, prepay your 2027 property tax bill by Dec. 31. Your county needs to have assessed the bill already.

Plante Moran estimates a single filer in the 35% bracket saves $14,140 by deducting the full $40,400. Check your AMT first, though. A large SALT deduction can trigger it. You also need enough total itemized deductions to beat your standard deduction.

The Section 199A deduction is permanent and equals up to 20% of qualified business income.

Medicine counts as a specified service business, so as your income increases, the deduction gets smaller before eventually disappearing.

The 2026 phase ranges from $201,750 to $276,750 for single filers, with double those amounts for joint filers. Part-time physicians, lower-earning specialties and couples with taxable income below $553,500 can still claim some deduction. Retirement contributions that lower your taxable income can pull you back into the range.

S corporation owners can take part of their income as distributions instead of salary, which avoids payroll taxes and the 0.9% Medicare tax. The IRS scrutinizes this closely, so make sure your salary is reasonable.

The OBBBA also lowered the cap on business losses that offset other income to $256,000 for single filers and $512,000 for joint filers in 2026. Rental income and losses count as passive unless you qualify as a real estate professional.

That status requires more than half of your personal services and more than 750 hours in property businesses. Special rules can help spouses meet material participation.

Equipment buyers can deduct 100% of the cost of qualifying property in the first year through bonus depreciation. This applies to property you acquire after Jan. 19, 2025. Section 179 expensing reached $2.56 million in 2026 and phases out above $4.09 million of purchases.

The equipment must be placed in service by Dec. 31.

Dec. 31 for most moves, including charitable gifts, payroll retirement deferrals and property tax prepayments. Self-employed physicians can set up and fund a retirement plan until the 2026 return due date, including extensions.

Add up your deductions and pick the larger amount. The standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers. Itemize when your SALT, mortgage interest and charitable gifts exceed it.

Defer if you expect the same or a lower tax rate next year. Accelerate if you expect a higher one. A fellow who starts as an attending in 2027 fits the second group.

It is 0.9% of wages above $200,000 for single filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. Employers start withholding at $200,000 regardless of your filing status, so couples often owe extra when they file.

Pay at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. Raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover any shortfall.

You can contribute $24,500 to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457 plan. Add $8,000 at age 50 or older. Ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 instead.

Employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages must make catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. If your plan has no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions.

Direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers. Most physicians use a backdoor Roth, which converts a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution of up to $7,500.

It affects early-retired and part-time physicians who buy marketplace coverage. Earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line and you lose all subsidies. CNBC reports the 2026 threshold at about $63,000 for a single person.

The cap is $40,400. It drops by 30 cents for every dollar of MAGI above $505,000 and bottoms out at $10,000 at about $606,333.

Often only in part. Medicine counts as a specified service business, so the deduction phases out between $201,750 and $276,750 of taxable income for single filers and disappears above that. Joint filers get double those amounts.

The 0.5% of AGI floor applies once per year, so one large gift loses less than several small ones. At $500,000 of AGI, a $50,000 gift saves $3,500 more than 5 yearly gifts of $10,000 at a 35% rate.

Yes. If you itemize and held the shares for more than 1 year, you deduct full market value and avoid the capital gains tax you’d owe on a sale. Donate publicly traded shares directly to the charity or donor-advised fund.

Yes. A CPA who knows your state and practice structure can model your return for you before you act.

The bonus-timing example is concrete: a $20,000 bonus paid Dec. 20 lands in 2026 wages, while a Jan. 5 pay date pushes the same dollars into 2027 and, at a 35% marginal rate, delays about $7,000 of federal tax for a year. Pairing that with the 2026 HSA ceilings ($4,400 self-only / $8,750 family, plus $1,000 catch-up at 55+) and the checklist on accelerating or deferring deductions gives employed physicians a short year-end punch list even when W-2 wages themselves are inflexible.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly free — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.
