Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

Another after thought, while nominal GDP matters for the annual deficit, that is not to say real GDP doesn’t matter in a silo. They both have relevance. Clearly the US government has more control over expenses, and to a somewhat lesser extent revenue, than it does inflation. For 2024, the deficit ran at 6.28% of GDP. If inflation, which most of us can agree above a low percentage is typically bad, drops back into a ~2% range but real GDP growth runs in the 2-3% range, which is decent growth, then we’re still only growing nominal GDP at 4-5% vs. 6%+ under the state-of-play. Anyway, another long rant but once again I just don’t like anything that tries to lead people by their emotions. Including the whole field of advertising.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

I disagree with the word “regressive.” It oversimplifies and is biased language. The thing is, the phenomenon you’re describing is simply an effect of a person being rich. The same percentage added to the sale of a good treats everyone equally – the difference is one person is rich. It’s not “hurting” the poorer person, it’s just that the rich person has a lot of money…because they’re rich. And when it comes to income taxes, “progressive” taxation is not more fair, it’s less fair. A percentage is already “progressive” because of math – 10% of $100,000 is $10,000 and 10% of $1 million is $100,000 – 10 times more tax revenue for 10 times the income. That’s completely fair. The idea of confiscating an escalating percentage is not more fair.

The math changes if you consider the marginal value of a dollar to someone who is rich vs someone who is poor. A thousand dollars more or less to someone making minimum wage is significant when measured in how much it will impact their lives. A thousand dollars more or less to a multi-millionaire with a high six figure income is barely noticeable. I agree that a simple percentage tax is more “fair” if what you’re measuring is dollars, but I think it’s less “fair” if what you’re measuring is impact on someone’s life. With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

Of course, if one’s goals are not to support and protect the USA and its people, then the above will seem silly and pointless (or even absurd!). A trade deficit means that the other countries are receiving more money than they are paying. But what do they then do with it? First, “they” here means the central banks of the other countries as the companies that receive the dollars for the stuff they sell to the US will trade it to the central bank for their local currency. So the central banks of the other countries are amassing an immense amount of dollars which they are not spending on buying US products due to the trade deficit. And judging from data from these central banks, they seem to be doing mainly one thing with these. Buying US treasury bonds. Which I find interesting, because these bonds will return more dollars which they then spend on buying more bonds because the US is not producing enough interesting-to-them goods or services to trade these dollars for.

Sounds like actually a good system from US perspective to me? And we all know how the US treasury bonds will be paid back when they come due. By selling more US treasury bonds. Which seem to be in good demand as the central banks of all the other countries want to put their dollars to use in some way.

I think I once heard a saying: If you owe 2 million dollars to the bank, the bank owns you. If you owe 2 trillion dollars, you own the bank.

Replace “you” by “US” and “bank” by “other countries” in that and the whole situation looks actually quite good from an US perspective to me. My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Nothing in residency prepared me for the cadaver head course. Severed heads rested face up in disposable roasting pans, lined down a row of tables, while surgeons calmly rehearsed facelifts. I kept my coffee down, though it was close.

Consider the advantages. These patients won’t ask about downtime or bring up a cousin’s botched eyelid job, and the state board will hear nothing from them. Somebody should study their satisfaction scores.

Medicine has always practiced on the dead, and for a long stretch it practiced on dead people who never agreed to the arrangement.

Nineteenth-century anatomy schools bought corpses from grave robbers and asked few questions about provenance. In Edinburgh in 1828, William Burke and William Hare decided digging was too slow, murdered sixteen people, and sold the bodies to anatomist Robert Knox.

Britain answered with the Anatomy Act of 1832, which handed medical schools the unclaimed bodies of the poor. Reform, of a sort.

Physicians have spent centuries trying to pin down the second a person stops being a person. We have never once nailed it.

In 1905, a French doctor named Beaurieux stood beside the guillotine as a convict named Languille lost his head. Beaurieux called out the man’s name. By his own report, the eyelids lifted and the eyes fixed on him before closing, and the trick worked a second time before it quit for good.

Consciousness or reflex? Nobody could say then, and we can’t now.

Cleveland, 1970. Neurosurgeon Robert White transplanted the head of one rhesus monkey onto the body of another, and the head woke up and tracked people around the room. White spent the rest of his career insisting the operation could work in humans.

I met my own version of this riddle at the bedside of a brain-dead organ donor. He was warm and pink. His heart pumped, his kidneys made urine, and at one point a spinal reflex lifted his arm off the sheet, the move clinicians call the Lazarus sign.

The nurse beside me didn’t flinch. I did. Legally he had died hours earlier, and the procurement team was already en route.

Hospice taught me the rest. Dying unfolds over hours or days, a slow dimming no monitor captures cleanly, yet the death certificate demands a single timestamp. So we pick one and move on.

For several centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up mummy as medicine. Physicians prescribed it for bruises, bleeding and a long menu of complaints, and when genuine Egyptian stock ran short, enterprising suppliers manufactured fresh “mummy” from whatever bodies they could find.

Folklore adds “mellified man,” a corpse supposedly steeped in honey for a century and sold by the chunk. Historians doubt he ever existed. I’ve seen supplement labels make bolder claims.

The dead, for all their weirdness, behave predictably. They stay where you put them. The living refuse that courtesy.

Beginning in the early 2000s, hundreds of children in Sweden withdrew into a state that looked like coma. Nearly all came from asylum-seeking families facing deportation.

They quit eating and talking, then quit opening their eyes, and some stayed that way for a year or longer while parents turned them in bed and nurses ran their feeding tubes. Swedish doctors named it uppgivenhetssyndrom. Resignation syndrome.

Scans came back clean, and so did the labs. Nobody found a virus, a toxin or a lesion. The condition clustered almost entirely inside Swedish borders, and many of the children surfaced slowly once their families won permission to stay.

That makes a lot of physicians squirm. The suffering is real, the paralysis is real, and the driver is a mind expressing despair in the shape its surroundings taught it to take.

I’ve watched a milder version play out in hospice more times than I can count. A patient holds steady for weeks, the family meeting goes sideways, and by the next morning he has stopped eating.

In the Kazakh village of Kalachi, starting around 2013, residents began dozing off mid-sentence. Some slept for days and woke with no memory of it. A shuttered Soviet uranium mine sat down the road, which made for a tidy villain.

Officials tested the air, water and soil, and the government eventually relocated much of the town. Plenty of clinicians point instead to a community watching its jobs and young people drain away, taking any sense of a future with them.

Le Roy, New York, ran a similar script in 2011. A cluster of high school girls developed tics, jerks and verbal outbursts that spread through the school and lit up the evening news.

Erin Brockovich showed up to investigate a chemical spill from a 1970 train derailment. Neurologists diagnosed conversion disorder, a label the families received with roughly the enthusiasm you’d expect.

I’ve delivered that diagnosis myself. The MRI was perfect, the legs still wouldn’t move, and the patient heard “it’s all in your head” no matter how carefully I phrased it. She left to find a doctor who would order another scan.

A toxin is a gift, because it blames no one. A functional diagnosis blames no one either, yet patients hear an accusation in it, and plenty of us deliver it like one. We fumble that conversation more often than we fumble a central line.

Among the Miskito people on Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast, young women fall prey to grisi siknis. They collapse, then bolt into the night, and later describe a dark stranger who came to carry them off.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Village healers treat it with rituals and herbs, and it hops from one community to the next like a bad cold.

Wealthy countries have their own spirits. In El Carmen de Bolívar, Colombia, in 2014, schoolgirls began fainting and convulsing after HPV vaccination. Videos of their episodes ricocheted across social media, and the country’s HPV vaccination rate collapsed.

Two years later, American diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds, and the press settled on a mysterious energy weapon. Some neurologists argue for a more mundane explanation that nobody in Washington wanted to hear.

Our culture supplies the toxins, the radio waves and the MRI that might at last catch the culprit. The Miskito get a dark stranger, while our demons come with CPT codes.

Funerals are where the haunted house collides with your financial plan. The National Funeral Directors Association put the 2023 median cost of a funeral with viewing and burial at about $8,300, and a funeral with cremation at roughly $6,280. Your aunt’s flower budget comes extra.

Whole-body donation to a medical school typically covers transport and cremation and returns the ashes to family, often at little or no cost. Programs vary, so call the school before you count on it.

Your body could spend its retirement crash-testing airbags or showing some nervous first-year where the brachial plexus hides. Mine would be in good company. I still owe that woman with the coral nail polish.

Physicians spend years making sure the 401(k) has a beneficiary. Few of us spend ten minutes deciding who gets the rest of the estate, meaning the part with the liver in it. Put it in writing this Halloween, somewhere between the will and the trust, and let your remains keep earning after you clock out.

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Free stock from a broker is real money, but a sign-up share is often worth a few dollars. The broker you pick may hold your investments for decades. Shortlist online brokers by their costs, the funds they sell, and the account you need, then take a free-stock offer only from a broker on your shortlist.

A sign-up share pays you once. The broker’s fees and choice of funds affect you every year you stay, and any charge for moving your account out comes due the day you leave.

You can get free stock four ways. Brokers give shares to new customers who open or fund an account, as Webull’s free-share offer does, and to current customers who refer friends. Stash’s Stock-Back debit card pays rewards in stock, and Acorns invests the rewards you earn shopping with its partner brands.

The shares tend to be small, and they come with conditions. Robinhood’s sign-up stock is worth $5 to $200, and about 99% of new customers get the minimum. You can sell the share after 3 trading days, but you can’t withdraw its cash value for 60 days. It also comes only with an individual taxable account, not an individual retirement account (IRA). Any tax on it is yours, and its value may show up on a 1099 tax form.

Skipping that order can turn a free share into a loss. Say you take an $8 share from a broker that doesn’t carry the funds you want and charges $75 to transfer an account out. Paying the fee to move the account leaves you $67 behind. A fractional free share, a slice of one share, can’t transfer to another broker, the brokerage regulator FINRA notes, so you’d have to sell it first.

Take a free share only from a broker you’d have opened without it.

One of the hard parts about financial planning is that you get plenty of at-bats at the little stuff, like spending money, investing, and saving, but not a lot of opportunities to practice the big stuff. When it comes to retirement, short of reincarnation, you get exactly one shot at it. Retirement is trial by fire. This is what makes the entire process so nerve-wracking.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Can you count on Social Security in retirement? While the retirement trust fund is projected to run out in 2032, according to the 2026 Trustees Report, benefits will still be paid out, just at a lower percentage. How much lower? 78% of scheduled benefits. That’s a 22% reduction, which is real. But it’s not a 100% reduction!

On average, heirs typically receive inherited IRAs at age 59, and the mean balance of those accounts is $128,000, according to a recent Vanguard report. Those accounts can be a sizable windfall, but taxes could take a chunk without proper planning, experts say. Original account owners may consider Roth conversions, strategic beneficiaries moves and other tactics.

When it comes to investing, people fixate on the risks of the stock market: What if the market crashes? Will I get the return I expected? How much can I draw down from investments each year without running out of money? Those are all valid concerns. But they are far from the only risks out there. What’s more, if you spend too much time focusing on just one risk then you are liable to make poor decisions.

The SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs are every money lesson in miniature: There’s the gap between the number on the screen and the money you can actually spend, the tax bill that stalks you home from the party, the way a big, sudden pile of money makes smart people stop thinking clearly. You don’t need stock options to learn any of that. You just need to see it laid out simply enough that the shame falls away.
